decisions.what: PROGRESS.json lives inside x-agent/.
decisions.why: Same reason as companion: two plugins in one repo.

decisions.what: Shared JSON Schemas are authored once in contract/schemas/ and vendored byte-identically into x-agent/schemas/ and x-companion/fixtures/schemas/.
decisions.why: Spec says vendor copies and treat companion spec as canonical on conflict; a single authored source with a drift test enforces that mechanically.

decisions.what: VERIFIED the current Claude Code plugin packaging format from the live docs before scaffolding, per operating_rules_for_implementing_agent. Fetched https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code/plugins-reference and https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code/plugins; BOTH now 301-redirect to code.claude.com, so the authoritative pages actually read were https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins-reference and https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins. Verified, verbatim from those pages: (1) the plugin manifest is `plugin.json` inside a `.claude-plugin/` directory at the plugin root; it is OPTIONAL, and if present only `name` is required (kebab-case, used as the skill namespace); common optional fields are displayName, version, description, author{name,email,url}, homepage, repository, license, keywords, plus component-path overrides skills/commands/agents/hooks/mcpServers/lspServers/outputStyles. (2) Skills are auto-discovered from a `skills/` directory at the PLUGIN ROOT as `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, each with YAML frontmatter whose keys include name, description, model, disable-model-invocation; the docs explicitly warn that skills/, commands/, agents/ and hooks/ must NOT be placed inside `.claude-plugin/` — only plugin.json goes there. (3) MCP servers are declared in `.mcp.json` at the plugin root (or inline under an `mcpServers` key in plugin.json) with the shape {"mcpServers":{"<id>":{"command":..., "args":[...], "env":{...}}}}, and the substitutions ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}, ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}, ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR} are available inside it. (4) `claude --plugin-dir ./x-agent` loads a plugin for local testing and `claude plugin validate ./x-agent` checks it. The scaffold matches this exactly: x-agent/.claude-plugin/plugin.json + x-agent/.mcp.json + x-agent/skills/wp-blocks/ (skill authored by the M7 track).
decisions.why: The spec forbids trusting memory for packaging. Recording the redirect chain matters: the docs.claude.com URLs named in the spec are no longer canonical.

decisions.what: The 16-tool table is declared in mcp/src/registry.ts and the six session/oracle/factory tools are loaded through a dynamic, failure-tolerant loader (loadExternalHandlers). The loader probes src/tools/<base>.{ts,js,mjs,mts} on disk with fs.existsSync and imports via pathToFileURL, so tsc never resolves a file that does not exist yet, and ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND / a syntax error / a module exporting no ToolDef all degrade to 'keep the not_implemented placeholder'.
decisions.why: Two agents implement tools in one package without editing each other's files, and `tools/list` must be complete (all 16, with schemas) before the second track's modules exist.

decisions.what: Every companion request carries the expected fingerprint in an `X-Expected-Fingerprint` request header, in addition to TreeIR.epoch on POST /validate.
decisions.why: CONTRACT.md §8 says 'every companion call carries the expected fingerprint' but only pins a mechanism for /validate (the tree's own epoch field). A request header is additive, ignored by any companion build that does not read it, and gives the mock a way to exercise the HTTP-409 epoch-conflict branch.

decisions.what: wp_validate and wp_spec_validate declare deliberately permissive MCP input schemas (z.looseObject with z.unknown().optional() fields carrying rich descriptions) and re-parse strictly inside the handler.
decisions.why: Both tools exist to REPORT schema violations as Diagnostics. A strict MCP input guard would turn every E_TREE_SCHEMA / E_SPEC_SCHEMA case into {code:'invalid_input'} and the tool would never be able to do its job. Handlers receive the original, unstripped arguments for the same reason.

decisions.what: W_UNQUANTIZED checks palette colours, spacing step sizes, typography sizes and layout.contentSize/wideSize against quantization_log[].snapped_to, compared as strings. Font FAMILIES are deliberately excluded.
decisions.why: The agent spec says 'tokens_candidates values all appear in quantization_log'. A font family is a chosen identifier, not a measured value snapped onto a scale, so requiring a quantization entry for it would be noise. Exported as quantizableValues() and asserted in tests.

decisions.what: E_BOX_OVERLAP slack is 2% of the PARENT box's width (for x/left-right) and height (for y/top-bottom), applied outward on all four edges. One diagnostic per offending child, listing every breached edge.
decisions.why: The spec says '2% slack' without naming the reference dimension; the parent is the only stable one (a zero-height child would otherwise get zero slack). Boundary behaviour is pinned by tests at slack+1 and slack-1.

decisions.what: wp_connect returns `suites` as plain slug strings (manifest.suites[].slug), dropping the version.
decisions.why: The spec pins the output type as `suites: string[]`. The versions remain available in full via wp_manifest.

decisions.what: wp_tokens_apply additionally returns `theme_json_preview` (the local emitter output) and `diff_against_instance`, and accepts `dry_run: true`.
decisions.why: The spec places templates/theme-json/emitter.ts on this side specifically 'for local preview/diff'. Surfacing it on the tool makes the extend-tier write rehearsable at zero cost and zero risk, which matters because the write is posture-gated and irreversible.

decisions.what: The build emits to mcp/dist/ with rootDir = the plugin root, so the server entry point is mcp/dist/mcp/src/server.js (referenced from .mcp.json). A `prepare` script runs the build on npm install, and no dist/ is left checked in.
decisions.why: templates/theme-json/emitter.ts lives outside mcp/ by spec, so rootDir must cover both; nesting is the honest consequence. A committed dist would silently go stale as the second track adds tool modules.

decisions.what: The vitest root is x-agent/ while the package is x-agent/mcp/; tsconfig maps the bare `vitest` specifier via compilerOptions.paths.
decisions.why: file_layout pins tests at x-agent/tests/ and the package at x-agent/mcp/. Node resolution cannot walk from x-agent/tests/ into x-agent/mcp/node_modules; Vitest self-aliases at runtime but tsc needs the explicit path mapping to type-check the suite.

decisions.what: tests/schemas.test.ts ships an inline JSON-Schema validator (no ajv) covering type/type-arrays, required, properties, additionalProperties, items, enum, const, pattern, minimum, exclusiveMinimum, oneOf and $ref (both #/definitions/... and the cross-file x-contract/<file>#/... form). It also asserts the vendored schemas use NO keyword outside that set.
decisions.why: The task pinned a smaller subset, but the vendored schemas actually use minimum/exclusiveMinimum/oneOf and a cross-file $ref (design-spec -> design-tokens). The keyword-coverage assertion means a future schema edit that introduces an unenforced keyword fails the suite instead of silently weakening the drift check.

decisions.what: Use @wp-playground/cli 3.1.50 via its exported runCLI() rather than shelling out to the wp-playground-cli binary.
decisions.why: Docker is installed but not running on this machine, so wp-env is not viable. runCLI({command:'server'}) returns a RunCLIServer with { playground, server, serverUrl } and an asyncDispose, which is what makes it possible to (a) run PHP inside the *same* instance that is serving HTTP and (b) tear down deterministically. Verified: package.json exports '.' -> index.js which re-exports runCLI from run-cli.d.ts; the type signature runCLI(args & {command:'server'}): Promise<RunCLIServer> is in node_modules/@wp-playground/cli/run-cli.d.ts.

decisions.what: Provision users and application passwords with playground.run({code}) after the server is up, not with a separate `wp-playground-cli php` process.
decisions.why: A separate CLI process is a different WordPress instance with a different database. Verified that playground.run() shares state with the HTTP request handler: created a user via run(), then authenticated as that user over HTTP with curl in the same boot and got 200. This works because the CLI's worker threads share a native site directory (bootRequestHandler takes nativeInternalDirPath and a FileLockManager).

decisions.what: Enable Application Passwords over plain http via a boot-generated mu-plugin filtering wp_is_application_passwords_available and wp_is_application_passwords_available_for_user to true.
decisions.why: WordPress gates Application Passwords on is_ssl(); the sandbox is http://127.0.0.1:<port>, so without the filter the whole Basic-auth half of CONTRACT.md is untestable. Generating the file from boot.mjs (rather than asking a human to place it) keeps the override scoped to the sandbox: it lives in tools/.runtime/work/<key>/mu-plugins/, is rewritten every boot, and never enters either plugin's source tree. Verified: with the filter, curl -u user:app_password against /wp/v2/users/me returns 200 and anonymous returns 401. Documented as sandbox-only in tools/README.md.

decisions.what: Inject X_COMPANION_POSTURE primarily through Playground's php.defineConstant() (RunCLIArgs.define), with a guarded mu-plugin as a second path.
decisions.why: Verified by experiment which mechanisms are visible to an HTTP request: --define/define (php.defineConstant) IS visible, and it applies before wp-config.php, i.e. earlier than mu-plugins and earlier than plugins; blueprint-level `constants` and a defineWpConfigConsts step with method rewrite-wp-config are also visible. Chose define because it needs no on-disk rewrite and survives a wiped site directory. The mu-plugin (000-x-posture.php, wrapped in if(!defined())) is the fallback for processes that do not go through the CLI's --define, which the CLI help explicitly calls process-specific. boot.mjs asserts the constant inside the sandbox after boot and refuses to return an instance whose posture does not match the request.

decisions.what: Mount plugin directories with the CLI's after-install `mount` (host dir -> /wordpress/wp-content/plugins/<dirname>) and activate them with an appended blueprint activatePlugin step.
decisions.why: Verified with --help on `server`: --mount takes /host/path:/vfs/path and is applied after WordPress installs but before blueprint steps run, so activatePlugin can see the mounted plugin. Verified the mount is a live filesystem view, not a copy: edited a mounted PHP file on the host mid-run and the next HTTP request returned the new behaviour with no restart. This is the property the plugin authors care about most.

decisions.what: Always mount a host directory at /wordpress via mount-before-install, so siteDir in the runtime JSON is a real path.
decisions.why: The `server` command otherwise keeps the site in a temp dir that is not exposed to the caller. Verified: with mount-before-install the WordPress install lands in the host dir (wp-load.php, wp-content/database present) and a second boot with wordpressInstallMode=install-from-existing-files-if-needed reuses it, cutting boot from ~7s to ~2.3s. --persist keeps the dir; without it the dir is wiped so the proof suite never inherits state.

decisions.what: Blueprint v1 declarations, validated against the schema validator shipped in @wp-playground/blueprints.
decisions.why: Step names and shapes were read out of node_modules/@wp-playground/blueprints/blueprint-schema.json (definitions.StepDefinition.oneOf) rather than guessed: activateTheme{themeFolderName}, setSiteOptions{options}, installPlugin{pluginData,options}, activatePlugin{pluginPath}, runPHP{code}, defineWpConfigConsts{consts,method}. Both profile blueprints were run through the package's own blueprint-schema-validator.js and report valid=true.

decisions.what: core-plus-suite installs Kadence Blocks with options.onError='throw' AND boot.mjs re-asserts the plugin is active afterwards.
decisions.why: The profile must fail loudly rather than silently degrade to core-only. Verified working online: 175 registered block types of which 59 are kadence/*. The double check means a future change in how a failed download is reported still cannot produce a mislabelled instance.

decisions.what: boot.mjs detaches by default: the parent spawns itself with --__daemon, waits on a ready file keyed by a boot id, prints the runtime JSON and exits.
decisions.why: The natural shell idiom is `RT=$(node tools/playground/boot.mjs ... --json)` followed by curl, which requires the booting process to exit while the server keeps serving. --foreground keeps the old behaviour for interactive use, and proof/lib/env.mjs boots in-process so withInstance can dispose deterministically.

decisions.what: Extend the CONTRACT.md §5 fallback trigger from '404' to '404 that is not a rest_* JSON error, or any 3xx'.
decisions.why: Measured against an instance booted with --permalinks plain: GET /wp-json/wp/v2/users/me returns 301 (WordPress canonical-redirects it), not 404, while /?rest_route=/wp/v2/users/me returns 200. A strict 404-only rule would never fall back on a plain-permalink site. The rest_* JSON check keeps a genuinely missing route (rest_no_route, which arrives as a 404 with a JSON body) from being misread as a permalink problem.

decisions.what: In proof/lib/env.mjs, authenticate the Playwright context with BOTH browser.newContext({httpCredentials}) and extraHTTPHeaders: { Authorization: Basic ... }.
decisions.why: httpCredentials alone does not authenticate a page navigation against WordPress, including with send:'always'. Chromium only replays Basic credentials after a 401 carrying WWW-Authenticate, and the WP REST API returns rest_forbidden 401s without that header. Measured: page.goto -> 401 with httpCredentials only (both with and without send/origin); 200 with the explicit header; context.request.get -> 200 either way, which is what makes the difference easy to miss. extraHTTPHeaders also covers sub-resource requests the harness page makes back to the REST API, which CONTRACT.md §6 requires.

decisions.what: Pin playwright to exactly 1.60.0.
decisions.why: Chromium build 1223 is already in ~/Library/Caches/ms-playwright on this machine, and 1.60.0 is the release that expects 1223 (checked playwright-core@<v>/browsers.json for 1.55-1.61: 1187/1194/1200/1208/1217/1223/1228). 1.62.1 wanted chromium-1234 and would have forced a browser download.

decisions.what: Probe port availability by binding the wildcard address, not 127.0.0.1.
decisions.why: Playground's Express server binds :: (dual stack). A probe bound to 127.0.0.1 reported an occupied port as free and the boot then died with EADDRINUSE on :::9400.

decisions.what: Flush stdout before process.exit() in wpcall.mjs and boot.mjs.
decisions.why: process.exit() truncates asynchronous pipe writes. A 947 KB /wp/v2/block-types response was being cut mid-JSON when piped to jq; writing through a callback and only then exiting fixes it.

decisions.what: Deterministic default ports 9400/9401/9402/9403 for core-only|core-plus-suite x toolchain|production, scanning to 9450 when taken.
decisions.why: The proof suite needs a production-posture instance running next to a toolchain one to assert posture_forbidden, and predictable ports make ad-hoc curl during development possible without reading the runtime file first.

decisions.what: Every tool-call transcript in SKILL.md and the two references is machine-verified against the real zod schemas, not eyeballed. A checker imports TOOLS from x-agent/mcp/dist/mcp/src/registry.js, extracts each '-> tool {json}' block from the markdown, structurally removes elision placeholders (block comments, and '...' strings that are whole array/object members - never '...' inside a real string value), runs inputSchema.safeParse on the arguments, and asserts every top-level key of each shown response exists in that tool's outputSchema shape. Final state: 22 tool calls checked, 0 problems.
decisions.why: A skill whose transcripts do not validate teaches the model to make invalid calls. This makes 'the examples are correct' a checkable claim instead of an assertion, and it caught real mistakes while writing (wp_tokens_apply takes the flattened DesignTokens fields; wp_validate/wp_compile take {version, epoch, blocks} flattened rather than a nested tree).

decisions.what: All example material is measured off live Playground instances rather than recalled: manifest attribute schemas, theme tokens, pattern names and shapes, diagnostic message text, and compiled markup (driven through GET /harness with Playwright). Read-only calls only, against instances already booted by other tracks on :9410 and :9430; nothing was mutated, nothing was stopped.
decisions.why: The whole premise of the plugin is 'the instance is ground truth, never training-data memory'. Documentation that violates that premise teaches the opposite of what it says. It also caught two things memory would have got wrong: core/heading no longer declares a textAlign attribute (alignment is style.typography.textAlign, and the instance answers W_ATTR_UNKNOWN), and the theme ships four testimonial patterns, which changes the R7 example from 'nothing exists' to the far more useful 'rungs 1 and 2 deliver everything except the rating'.

decisions.what: bin/plugin-check.sh runs Plugin Check through @wp-playground/cli's `php` subcommand rather than its `wp-cli` Blueprint step. The step exists and works, but @wp-playground/cli 3.1.50 does not print what it captured, so `run-blueprint` with a wp-cli step produces an empty report. The script instead mounts a tiny run-cli.php that sets $GLOBALS['argv'] and requires /tmp/wp-cli.phar (put there by the Blueprint's extraLibraries:['wp-cli']), and runs it via `wp-playground-cli php -- /wordpress/x-plugin-check/run-cli.php`, which does stream stdout and stderr.
decisions.why: M7 asks for an observed `wp plugin check x-companion` result. WP-CLI is not installed on this machine and Docker is not running, so Playground is the only real path; and a check whose output you cannot read is not a check. Verified end to end: `wp plugin list` and `wp plugin check` both produce their real output through this route.

decisions.what: plugin-check.sh scans the DISTRIBUTION surface by default, passing --exclude-directories=tests,bin,fixtures to `wp plugin check`; --include-dev scans everything. Both numbers are recorded in deviations[].
decisions.why: Those three directories are development scaffolding that never ships to wordpress.org, and Plugin Check flags any .sh file at all as `application_detected` ('Application files are not permitted') - it flags this very script, and tests/run-all.sh, and fixtures/packages/build.sh. Scanning them makes the report describe a plugin nobody would ever submit. The exclusion is stated in the script header, printed to stderr on every run, and documented in x-companion/README.md, so the number is never presented without its scope.

decisions.what: x-companion/readme.txt is written to the wordpress.org readme standard (header block, Description, Installation, FAQ, Changelog) with `Tested up to: 7.1`.
decisions.why: Plugin Check reports `no_plugin_readme` as an ERROR without the file, and then `outdated_tested_upto_header` when the value trails the WordPress version the checker sees. The sandbox boots `--wp latest`, which currently resolves to 7.1; 6.9 produced 'Tested up to: 6.9 < 7.1'. This value must be bumped whenever the target WordPress moves - it is a release chore, not a constant.

decisions.what: SKILL.md's R7 worked example scaffolds `agent/testimonial-card`, not `agent/testimonial`.
decisions.why: `agent/testimonial` is already used by the factory track's live fixture (fixtures/trees/valid-with-agent-block.json and the M5 live test), with a different attribute set. Two documents describing the same block name with different attributes is worse than two clearly different blocks. tree-ir.md 7 documents `agent/testimonial` as measured from a live instance while that fixture was installed; SKILL.md 5 scaffolds a distinct block whose justification is the star rating.

decisions.what: The warm session launches chromium lazily and opens GET /harness even more lazily. `create()` allocates nothing; `page()` (used by wp_verify/wp_screenshot) starts the browser; only `compile()` loads the harness.
decisions.why: GET /harness was returning 501 not_implemented while this track was being built. Making the oracle depend on the harness would have blocked M4 behind M3 for no reason — and in production it means a companion build without a harness still gives you a working verifier.

decisions.what: wp_compile probes GET /fingerprint on EVERY call (ctx.manifestCache.get({fingerprintMinIntervalMs: 0})) instead of accepting the 10 s rate limit.
decisions.why: CONTRACT.md §5 calls /fingerprint the cheap route that runs 'before every batch', and a compile is a batch. Measured: one extra request per compile against a Playground instance. The alternative is compiling at a stale epoch for up to 10 s after a plugin toggle, which is exactly the failure the epoch discipline exists to prevent — and it is what makes the M3 auto-reload acceptance deterministic rather than timing-dependent.

decisions.what: The wp_verify render shell loads the site homepage's inline <style> blocks as well as its <link> stylesheets, always, not only when /render.enqueued_styles is empty.
decisions.why: The spec says 'if enqueued_styles is empty, harvest the homepage'. On a block theme enqueued_styles is NEVER empty (block stylesheets are enqueued) but it also never contains the design system: wp_enqueue_global_styles emits every --wp--preset--* custom property INLINE, which /render cannot report as a URL. Measured on the golden landing: 7 stylesheets and 23 inline style blocks; without the inline half every colour, font size and spacing token measures as an unstyled default and the oracle is worthless. Harvest is still once per fingerprint, as specified.

decisions.what: The homepage harvest is a Playwright navigation in the warm browser, not an HTTP request.
decisions.why: context.ts note 3 forbids `fetch` outside companion.ts, and companion.ts has no 'GET the homepage' method (it is not a companion route). Navigating the page we already have both respects the rule and gets the post-JS DOM.

decisions.what: block_name is resolved by inverting the manifest's own key set through wp.blocks.getBlockDefaultClassName ('core/x' -> 'wp-block-x', 'ns/x' -> 'wp-block-ns-x'), never by string-surgery on the class.
decisions.why: Only the manifest can disambiguate 'wp-block-kadence-rowlayout' into 'kadence/rowlayout' rather than 'kadence-rowlayout'. It also means the map is correct for agent/* blocks the instant they are installed, with no table to maintain.

decisions.what: A region's 'gap' is read from computed row-gap when there is one and otherwise MEASURED as the median spacing between element children.
decisions.why: WordPress implements blockGap as a margin on children for flow and constrained layouts. The computed `gap` there is `normal`, so a naive reading reports 'no gap' for every core/group on the page.

decisions.what: 'One spacing step' (the gap tolerance) = snap the expected value onto the spec's own spacing scale, then take the distance from that step to its nearest neighbour on the same scale.
decisions.why: The spec pins 'gap 1 spacing-step' without saying which step. Any fixed number would be wrong on a scale that is not linear (Twenty Twenty-Five's is clamp()-based and very much not linear). This definition means 'closer than the smallest distinguishable move on your own scale' — i.e. a rounding, not a design decision.

decisions.what: A region's font_size is the LARGEST computed font size in its subtree.
decisions.why: A region-level font_size_slug names the region's type scale, which in practice is its headline. Averaging or taking the region element's own font-size measures the wrapper, which is usually inherited body copy and never changes.

decisions.what: Region-to-element matching is geometry-dominant with role and accessible-name bonuses, greedy over a DFS of the spec, with a hard constraint that a child region must match inside its parent's matched element. Threshold 0.35.
decisions.why: The spec says 'role heuristics + order + a11y name'. Role alone is far too weak (every section is a core/group) and order alone breaks the moment a region is missing. Geometry is the only signal that is always present; role and name break its ties. Measured scores on the golden landing: 1.539-1.550 for all six regions, i.e. an enormous margin above threshold.

decisions.what: 'extra' diffs are emitted only for top-level (minimum-depth) named block wrappers with no matching region.
decisions.why: Every nested wrapper would otherwise be 'extra' and a 26-node page would report ~20 extras that no spec was ever going to describe.

decisions.what: A colour tolerance of 8/255 per channel was added as `tolerances.color_channel` (default 8). It is the one tolerance the spec does not pin.
decisions.why: kind:'color' is in the required diff enum, so colour has to be diffable, and an exact-match rule would fail on 8-bit rounding and sub-pixel compositing. 8/255 is below the smallest deliberate palette step in any theme.json seen here and above every rendering artefact measured.

decisions.what: Live tests are opt-in via X_AGENT_LIVE=1 and must be run with --no-file-parallelism.
decisions.why: vitest's include is tests/**/*.test.ts, so without the gate a plain `npx vitest run` would need a WordPress and a browser. And compile.test.ts deliberately moves the instance's fingerprint, so running the live files concurrently against one instance makes them fight.

decisions.what: oracle.ts ships installEvalShims(page), which defines a no-op globalThis.__name before any large page.evaluate.
decisions.why: tsx/esbuild transpile with keepNames, which rewrites `const f = () => {}` into `__name(() => {}, 'f')`. The helper lives in the Node module scope, so the function body Playwright ships into the page throws ReferenceError: __name is not defined. A tsc build never hits this; every test run does. The shim argument is a string literal so esbuild cannot touch it.

decisions.what: The Playground smoke test runs in a CHILD node process (`.x-agent-build/smoke/smoke-runner.mjs`, generated at run time), configured through a JSON file and answering through a JSON file. Its stdout/stderr are piped into the build log and never touch the parent's.
decisions.why: This process's stdout is the MCP stdio transport. @wp-playground/cli boots worker threads and an Express server and is under no obligation to keep quiet on fd 1, and a PHP-wasm fatal is a real crash. A child process makes both harmless: nothing it prints can corrupt the MCP wire and nothing it crashes can take the server down. It also makes teardown unconditional.

decisions.what: The smoke runner contains no PHP and no regexes. factory.ts generates the two PHP probes (registrationProbePhp, renderProbePhp) and hands them over in the config; the runner boots, runs them, and returns raw text; the parent parses the tagged payload and extracts any PHP diagnostic (readTagged, extractPhpError, interpretSmoke — all unit-tested offline).
decisions.why: The first cut embedded PHP inside a JS template literal inside a TS template literal and needed three levels of escaping to survive. A runner that only forwards bytes cannot be wrong about a PHP fatal, and every parsing rule stays testable without booting WordPress.

decisions.what: The smoke test speaks no HTTP at all. Both `GET /wp/v2/block-types` and `POST /wp/v2/block-renderer/{name}` are dispatched INSIDE the sandbox with `rest_do_request()` after `wp_set_current_user(1)`, and `do_blocks()` is run as a cross-check. `rendered_html` prefers the REST block-renderer output and falls back to do_blocks.
decisions.why: Honours the seam contract's 'NEVER write fetch outside companion.ts' without needing an exception, and skips all Basic-auth plumbing against a throwaway instance. It is still genuinely the sandbox's REST layer — the same controller a real editor calls.

decisions.what: The bytes that get smoke-tested and the bytes that get zipped are the same bytes. stagePackage() copies block.json, the render file, every `file:` reference in block.json and the sibling `index.asset.php` into `<dir>/.x-agent-build/plugin/<slug>/`, writes the one-line loader plugin next to it, and the sandbox mounts that directory as a plugin. packageBlock() then zips that same `<slug>` directory.
decisions.why: A smoke test that runs the working tree proves nothing about the package. This way node_modules, src/ and package.json are provably not in the tested artefact, and 'it worked in the sandbox' means 'this zip worked'.

decisions.what: wp_block_build_test RETURNS its failures as {built, smoke:{registered, rendered_html, php_error?}, failure:{code:'build_failed'|'smoke_failed', message, hint}} instead of throwing an XError.
decisions.why: The spec output shape and the M5 acceptance both require reading `smoke.php_error` on the failure path, which an error envelope cannot carry. The CONTRACT.md §7 codes build_failed / smoke_failed are preserved verbatim in failure.code, so nothing is lost. Bad ARGUMENTS (missing dir, no block.json, static block.json) still throw invalid_input as usual.

decisions.what: Dependency cache: `<workspace>/.deps/<sha256(devDependencies)[0:16]>/node_modules` plus its package-lock.json. The first scaffold installs normally, then its node_modules is MOVED into the cache and symlinked back; later scaffolds with the same dependency set get the symlink and `npm ci` is used when the cached lockfile applies. `X_AGENT_BLOCK_CACHE=0` opts out; `force_install: true` forces a fresh install.
decisions.why: A cold `npm install` of @wordpress/scripts is ~1529 packages and 44 s. Keying by the devDependencies hash means a changed @wordpress/scripts range gets a fresh install rather than a stale tree. Measured: 56.5 s cold, 11.1 s warm.

decisions.what: wp_block_install re-reads the zip and checks it against the ENTIRE CONTRACT.md §5 install policy locally, before the posture probe and before any POST. A violation is {code:'invalid_input'} carrying `reasons: string[]`.
decisions.why: The companion answers 422 block_policy with the same reasons list. A round trip to a real instance should never be how the agent first learns that its own package is malformed, and the same inspector runs on our own output inside wp_block_build_test.

decisions.what: The posture gate reads `GET /fingerprint` (introspect tier, non-mutating) FIRST and throws errPostureForbidden('/blocks/install') before the multipart body is built. CompanionClient.installBlockBytes has its own assertToolchain guard; this one is in front of it.
decisions.why: The requirement is 'send NOTHING that would mutate', which is a stronger promise than 'the far end refuses it'. The client-side guard only fires once posture is already known, so something has to establish it, and /fingerprint is the cheap route the contract designates for exactly this.

decisions.what: The live sabotage test proves 'nothing was sent' two ways: (a) structurally — the Runtime it uses has no resolvable connection config at all, demonstrated in the same test by calling wp_manifest on it and asserting {code:'invalid_input', message:/Missing connection config/}; wp_block_build_test is `local: true`, so any attempt to reach an instance would have surfaced the same way. (b) observationally — broken-card never appears in GET /blocks/library and no pre-existing entry disappears.
decisions.why: (a) is race-free and is the real proof. The exact library-equality check that (b) started as was flaky: the toolchain instance is shared with other tracks' live suites in this repo and another suite legitimately installed `testimonial@1.0.0` mid-test. Asserting 'ours never appears, theirs never disappears' is the assertion that actually means something on a shared instance.

decisions.what: The live suite is gated on `X_AGENT_FACTORY_LIVE=1`, not the generic `X_AGENT_LIVE=1` the M3/M4 live suite uses.
decisions.why: Observed in practice: another track ran `X_AGENT_LIVE=1 npx vitest run ../tests/live` and picked up this file, which installs a block onto a real instance and moves its epoch underneath their tests. Vitest's root is x-agent/ and every track shares it, so a suite with side effects on a shared instance must have its own switch.

decisions.what: block.json lives at the SCAFFOLD ROOT (not src/), carries `editorScript: file:./build/index.js` and `render: file:./render.php`, and wp-scripts keeps its default `src/index.js` entry.
decisions.why: The install policy requires block.json at the block root of the zip. Keeping it out of src/ also stops wp-scripts' block.json auto-entry detection from firing, so the build stays the plain single-entry webpack build and its output shape is predictable.

decisions.what: adm-zip is bound through `createRequire(import.meta.url)` behind a hand-written minimal interface, exported as `loadAdmZip(): ZipCtor`. @wp-playground/cli is located by walking up from the module looking for `node_modules/@wp-playground/cli/index.js` or `tools/node_modules/@wp-playground/cli/index.js`, with an `X_AGENT_PLAYGROUND_CLI` override.
decisions.why: adm-zip ships no .d.ts and @types/adm-zip is not installed; @wp-playground/cli is installed under tools/node_modules, which Node resolution from x-agent/mcp/src cannot reach. mcp/package.json is not this track's file to edit, so both are resolved at runtime instead of by adding dependencies. `tsc --noEmit` stays clean and nothing is typed `any`.

decisions.what: The smoke sandbox binds the first free port in 9440-9449, overridable with X_AGENT_SMOKE_PORT_RANGE ("9460-9469") or pinned with X_AGENT_SMOKE_PORT / the tool's `port` argument. Timeouts: X_AGENT_BLOCK_BUILD_TIMEOUT_MS (default 15 min) and X_AGENT_BLOCK_SMOKE_TIMEOUT_MS (default 5 min), each overridable per call via timeout_ms / smoke_timeout_ms.
decisions.why: Several agents share this machine and tools/README.md splits the port space. The build timeout has to tolerate a cold ~1500-package npm install on a slow network, so it is generous by default and configurable, as required.

decisions.what: The factory is registered with `registerFactoryProvider({ create: (ctx) => new BlockFactory(ctx.logger) })` at the top of mcp/src/factory.ts, and the tool handlers reach it with `asFactory(await getFactory(ctx))`. No file owned by the core track was edited.
decisions.why: Seam contract note 2(b) in context.ts. Lazy construction, and wp_disconnect disposes it for free.

decisions.what: The interop proof suite (proof/) drives the REAL MCP tool entrypoint callTool() against a REAL Playground WordPress, never the mock companion.
decisions.why: The mock proves the client's own logic; it cannot prove the two plugins interoperate. Every P-scenario therefore boots a live instance with x-companion actually activated.

ROOT CAUSE, found and confirmed, and it is NOT in this track. An installed agent block lives in `wp_upload_dir()['basedir']/x-agent-blocks/{slug}/` per CONTRACT.md §5. WordPress's register_block_script_handle() builds a script's URL with plugins_url(), which only understands wp-content/plugins (and, since 6.4, theme dirs). That 404s, so registerBlockType never runs client-side, __registry() lacks agent/pricing-card, and wp_compile correctly reports harness_gap rather than serialising something wrong. The block itself is fine: it IS in the harness's server-side bootstrap, it IS in /wp/v2/block-types, and POST /render produces the right HTML. The fix belongs in x-companion, where the block is registered — e.g. filter the metadata's script URL (block_type_metadata_settings / register_block_type_args) to point at wp_upload_dir()['baseurl'] for blocks it installed. Nothing in the agent-side factory can correct it.

deviations.what: KNOWN LIMITATION, environment-level, does not affect any M5 acceptance: on a single long-lived Playground instance, INSTALL AFTER DELETE fails with HTTP 500 install_failed 'Could not move the extracted block into the library.' First install and repeat install (the replace path) both work.
deviations.detail: Reproduced deterministically on a freshly booted core-only/toolchain instance with one script: install #1 -> 200 replaced_previous:false; install #2 -> 200 replaced_previous:true; DELETE -> 200 with the epoch restored exactly; install #3 (identical zip, seconds later) -> 500 install_failed. Afterwards the host filesystem shows uploads/x-agent-blocks/ EMPTY and the x_companion_block_library option is [], so nothing is stale on the host or in the database — the stale state is inside the sandbox. tools/playground/boot.mjs runs `wp-playground-cli server` with 6 worker threads, each with its own PHP-wasm NODEFS view of the mounted /wordpress directory; a directory rename performed by one worker is not reflected in another's cached nodes, and requests round-robin across workers, so the rename() inside WP_Filesystem_Direct::move() fails for the worker that handles the next install. Making it worse by hand confirms the direction: deleting uploads/x-agent-blocks/ on the HOST while the instance runs makes even wp_mkdir_p() fail ('Could not create /wordpress/wp-content/uploads/x-agent-blocks'), which is only possible if the worker is reading a cached node rather than the host. Candidate fixes, both outside this track: boot Playground with `workers: 1` for install-heavy scenarios (runCLI accepts it; boot.mjs does not currently expose it), or have x-companion fall back to a recursive copy+unlink when rename() fails.
